questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A playbook converts 6.3 x 10^1; explain why result is 63.

answer.exemplar: Positive exponent moves decimal right one place: 63. Moving left would give 0.63, wrong.

questions.explanation: Applying the scientific notation to standard form rule — Positive exponent moves right — yields "Positive exponent moves decimal right one place: 63". Reversing the reasoning would recover the given quantities.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A coach converts 920; explain why scientific notation is 9.2 x 10^2.

answer.exemplar: Move decimal two places left to get 9.2, exponent 2. Using 92 x 10^1 would not be standard.

questions.explanation: The standard form to scientific notation principle here is: Decimal after first digit. On that basis "Move decimal two places left to get 9" is correct.

questions.stem: A playbook converts 0.0008; explain why it is 8 x 10^{-4}.

answer.exemplar: Move decimal four places right to get 8, exponent -4. Positive exponent would be wrong.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this converting between forms item is: Negative exponent for small. That is why "Move decimal four places right to get 8, exponent -4" is the answer.

questions.stem: A coach writes sqrt(x) = x^{1/2}; explain why.

answer.exemplar: A square root asks what squared gives x, matching exponent 1/2 since (x^{1/2})^2=x. Using exponent 2 would square instead.

questions.explanation: Applying the roots and fractional exponents rule — Root degree denominator — yields "A square root asks what squared gives x, matching exponent 1/2 since (x^{1/2})^2=x". Reversing the reasoning would recover the given quantities.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A playbook simplifies sqrt(18); explain why result is 3 sqrt(2).

answer.exemplar: sqrt(18)=sqrt(9*2)=3sqrt2. Leaving as sqrt18 would not be simplified.

questions.explanation: The simplifying radicals principle here is: Factor perfect square. On that basis "sqrt(18)=sqrt(9*2)=3sqrt2" is correct.

questions.stem: A coach adds 2 sqrt(7) + 3 sqrt(7); explain why result is 5 sqrt(7).

answer.exemplar: Like radicals combine by adding coefficients: 2+3=5. Adding radicands would give sqrt14, wrong.

questions.explanation: Add coefficients. The computation rests on add coefficients. Working backward through the relation confirms the value.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A playbook divides sqrt(20)/sqrt(5); explain why result is 2.

answer.exemplar: sqrt(20)/sqrt(5)=sqrt(4)=2. Subtracting radicands gives sqrt15, wrong.

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this ratio of radicals item is: Divide radicands. That is why "sqrt(20)/sqrt(5)=sqrt(4)=2" is the answer.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: In a standardized integrated mathematics I assessment, a coach writes 2^{-3}=1/8; explain why.

answer.exemplar: Negative exponent means reciprocal: 1/2^3=1/8. Negating would give -8, wrong.

questions.explanation: Reciprocate base. The rule reciprocate base gives the value. A quick check with the given numbers returns the same value.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A coach multiplies m^3 * m^5; what is the result?

options.text: m to the fifteenth, multiplying exponents
options.misconception: confuses "m to the fifteenth, multiplying exponents" with the correct "m to the eighth, adding exponents"

options.text: Two m to the eighth, doubling base
options.misconception: confuses "Two m to the eighth, doubling base" with the correct "m to the eighth, adding exponents"

options.text: m to the second, subtracting exponents
options.misconception: subtracts exponents

options.text: m to the eighth, adding exponents

questions.explanation: The product of powers principle here is: Add exponents. On that basis "m to the eighth, adding exponents" is correct, while "m to the fifteenth, multiplying exponents" confuses "m to the fifteenth, multiplying exponents" with the correct "m to the eighth, adding exponents".

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A playbook divides n^9 / n^4; what is the result?

options.text: n to the fifth, subtracting exponents
n to the thirty-six, multiplying exponents
options.misconception: selects "n to the thirty-six, multiplying exponents" instead of "n to the fifth, subtracting exponents"

options.text: n to the thirteenth, adding exponents
options.misconception: names "n to the thirteenth, adding exponents" where the rule requires "n to the fifth, subtracting exponents"

options.text: n to the negative five, reversing
options.misconception: reverses subtraction

questions.explanation: For a quotient of powers question like this, the governing rule is: Subtract exponents. Applying it makes "n to the fifth, subtracting exponents" correct. The alternative "n to the thirteenth, adding exponents" is wrong because it names "n to the thirteenth, adding exponents" where the rule requires "n to the fifth, subtracting exponents".

questions.stem: A coach computes (p^4)^2; what is the result?

options.text: p to the fourth squared, not simplified
options.misconception: leaves unsimplified

options.text: p to the eighth, multiplying exponents
p to the sixteenth, squaring exponent
options.misconception: names "p to the sixteenth, squaring exponent" where the rule requires "p to the eighth, multiplying exponents"

options.text: p to the sixth, adding exponents
options.misconception: confuses "p to the sixth, adding exponents" with the correct "p to the eighth, multiplying exponents"

questions.explanation: The rule that settles this power of a power item is: Multiply exponents. That is why "p to the eighth, multiplying exponents" is right. The option "p to the fourth squared, not simplified" (leaves unsimplified) does not satisfy the rule.

questions.subject: INTEGRATED_1
questions.stem: A playbook writes (4k)^2; what is the result?

options.text: Four k squared, squaring only k
options.misconception: squares only variable
squares only coefficient

options.text: Sixteen k squared, squaring both factors

options.misconception: multiplies coefficient by exponent

questions.explanation: Applying the power of a product rule — Square each factor — yields "Sixteen k squared, squaring both factors". The tempting "Four k squared, squaring only k" fails because it squares only variable.

questions.stem: A coach computes (ab)^0 for nonzero a and b; what is the value?

options.misconception: keeps base — treating "ab, keeping base" as the answer
confuses with zero
names "Undefined, base includes zero" where the rule requires "One, any nonzero base to zero is one"

options.text: One, any nonzero base to zero is one

questions.explanation: For a zero exponents question like this, the governing rule is: Zero exponent yields one. Applying it makes "One, any nonzero base to zero is one" correct. The alternative "ab, keeping base" is wrong because it keeps base — treating "ab, keeping base" as the answer.
